items.title: How to Export AWS CloudTrail Logs
items.summary: For the last 90 days of management events, use the CloudTrail console ( Event history → Download events → JSON ) or aws cloudtrail lookup-events. For anything older, or for data events like S3 object reads, read your trail’s log files in S3. They sit under s3:// /AWSLogs/ /CloudTrail/ /YYYY/MM/DD/. CloudTrail is the audit log of your AWS control plane: every console login, every API call, every role assumption. In a cloud incident, it’s the first thing everyone asks for. Prime Core has 262 detection rules for CloudTrail, mapped to 177 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Among them: misuse of cloud accounts (T1078.004), attackers switching off cloud logging (T1562.008) and data theft from cloud storage (T1530). Before you start Event history and trails are different things. Event history is always on and free. It keeps 90 days of management events, per region. A trail is something you configure: it writes to S3, keeps logs as long as you like, and can include data events. Check what you have: aws cloudtrail describe-trails aws cloudtrail get-trail-status --name IsLogging: false on a trail that should be running is a finding in itself. Regions matter. Event history is per region, and events from global services like IAM usually land in us-east-1. If you’re looking for a CreateUser call in eu-west-1, you won’t find it. Permissions. cloudtrail:LookupEvents for event history. For trail files, s3:ListBucket and s3:GetObject on the bucket, plus kms:Decrypt if the trail is encrypted with a KMS key. Option 1: Console download Open CloudTrail, go to Event history , set the time range and any filters (event name, user, resource), then choose Download events → JSON . The download respects your filters, so check them first. It covers the current region only. Option 2: lookup-events from the CLI aws cloudtrail lookup-events --region us-east-1 \ --start-time 2026-10-19T00:00:00Z --end-time 2026-10-20T00:00:00Z \ --output json > ct_use1_1019.json Two things to know. First, each result wraps the actual event as a JSON string in CloudTrailEvent. Unwrap it into one clean event per line: jq -c '.Events[].CloudTrailEvent | fromjson' ct_use1_1019.json > ct_use1_1019.jsonl Second, lookup-events is rate limited per account and region, and it accepts only one –lookup-attributes filter per call. Wide time windows take a while, so narrow them where you can. To cover every region, loop over aws ec2 describe-regions –query ‘Regions[].RegionName’ –output text. Option 3: Trail files from S3 This is the route for history beyond 90 days and for data events: aws s3 cp s3://my-trail-bucket/AWSLogs/123456789012/CloudTrail/eu-west-1/2026/10/19/ ./ct/ --recursive gunzip ./ct/*.json.gz jq -c '.Records[]' ./ct/*.json > ct_euw1_1019.jsonl Each file holds a Records array, and the jq line flattens all of them into one event per line. Organization trails add the organization ID to the path: AWSLogs/ / /CloudTrail/…. If you use CloudTrail Lake, you can run SQL over your events and save the results instead. Open logtotal.com and drop in the .jsonl (or .json file). Sanitize. [what gets masked: account IDs, ARNs, IPs, access key IDs, usernames]. Look it over before you continue. Review. items.title: How to Export Microsoft Entra ID Sign-in Logs
items.summary: In the Microsoft Entra admin center, open Identity → Monitoring & health → Sign-in logs , set your filters, and choose Download → JSON . For bigger or scripted pulls, use Microsoft Graph: GET /auditLogs/signIns. Either way, you only get what’s still retained: 7 days on Entra ID Free, 30 days with P1 or P2. Sign-in logs show who authenticated, from where, to which app, and whether MFA and Conditional Access held. In identity-driven attacks, that’s most of the story. Prime Core has 170 detection rules for Entra ID sign-in data, mapped to 113 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Among them: password spraying (T1110.003), MFA fatigue (T1621) and logins with stolen cloud credentials (T1078.004). Get Started for Free Before you start Retention is short. If the activity you’re after is older than 7 or 30 days, the portal and Graph won’t have it. The only place it might still exist is wherever your diagnostic settings send sign-in logs: a Log Analytics workspace, Microsoft Sentinel or a storage account. See our [Microsoft Sentinel export guide] for that route. Roles. Reports Reader is the least-privileged role that can read sign-in logs. Security Reader and Global Reader work too. There are four kinds of sign-ins. Interactive user, non-interactive user, service principal and managed identity each have their own tab in the portal. Token replay and abuse of refresh tokens tend to show up under non-interactive , which people forget to export. Option 1: Download from the portal Go to Sign-in logs and pick the tab (start with interactive, then non-interactive). Set Date and any filters (user, application, status). Choose Download , then JSON . The portal limits how many records a single download includes. [PROOF: confirm the current limit.] For large ranges, split by day or use Graph. Option 2: Microsoft Graph PowerShell This pulls raw API JSON, follows paging, and writes one sign-in per line: Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "AuditLog.Read.All" $uri = "https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/auditLogs/signIns?`$filter=createdDateTime ge 2026-10-19T00:00:00Z and createdDateTime lt 2026-10-20T00:00:00Z" do { $page = Invoke-MgGraphRequest -Method GET -Uri $uri -OutputType Json | ConvertFrom-Json $page.value | ForEach-Object { $_ | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress } | Add-Content signins_1019.jsonl $uri = $page.'@odata.nextLink' } while ($uri) The v1.0 endpoint returns interactive sign-ins. Non-interactive and service principal sign-ins need the beta endpoint with a signInEventTypes filter. Reading sign-ins through the API also depends on your tenant’s license tier. Timestamps are UTC throughout. What to look for Field or value What it tells you status.errorCode 50126 Wrong username or password. Many of these across many users means spraying status.errorCode 50053 Account locked by smart lockout status.errorCode 500121 MFA failed or was denied; a burst of these is MFA fatigue clientAppUsed = IMAP, POP, SMTP, “Other clients” Legacy authentication that skips MFA conditionalAccessStatus Whether CA applied, passed or failed riskLevelDuringSignIn, location, ipAddress Risky or unfamiliar origins The pattern worth stopping for: a string of 50126 failures across many accounts from one IP range, then a success for one of them. Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the JSON file. Sanitize. [what gets masked: UPNs, display names, IPs, device names, tenant and object IDs]. Look it over before you continue. Review. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix Nothing older than a week or a month Retention for your license tier Check Log Analytics, Sentinel or storage if diagnostic settings were on Graph returns 403 Missing AuditLog.Read.All consent, role or license Grant consent; check your role and tenant license Export has only interactive sign-ins Other types live in separate tabs, or in beta Graph Export each tab; use the beta endpoint Download contains fewer records than the portal shows Portal download limit Split by day, or use Graph FAQ What about Entra audit logs? Those are a different log: directory changes like new users, role assignments and app consents. Same portal area, Audit logs. In Graph it’s /auditLogs/directoryAudits. In an incident, you usually want both. Can I get sign-ins from Sentinel instead? Yes, if the Entra ID connector is on: they’re in the SigninLogs and AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs tables, with whatever retention your workspace has.

Capcom warns users not to follow URLs or open attachments in suspicious messages. You can also take these steps: Enable CAPCOM ID’s two-factor authentication: This adds an authenticator-app code to the sign-in process, helping protect your account if someone obtains your password. Set it up from your Account page using a smartphone or tablet. Capcom recommends Google Authenticator or Microsoft Authenticator. Check your account, especially if you received an unexpected password-change notice: Review your registered information and linked platform accounts from your Account page. items.title: Node.js Patches Brotli Remote Code Execution Flaw: Find Vulnerable Runtimes Before Attackers Do
items.summary: Executive Summary On October 21, 2026, Node.js released fixes for 10 vulnerabilities across its three supported release lines: 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x. Four are rated High. The most severe, CVE-2026-111497, is an out-of-bounds write in the bundled Brotli decoder that Node.js says permits remote code execution. These flaws live in the Node.js runtime itself, not in application packages, so dependency checks will not surface them. Qualys customers can find affected runtimes across hosts, containers, and cloud workloads, including copies outside standard install paths, prioritize those exposed to the internet, and confirm each fix after patching. Why This Release Needs Attention Now The four high-severity vulnerabilities impact two areas that nearly every Node.js service interacts with: compressed data and outbound connections. CVE-2026-111497 is a vulnerability found in the code responsible for decompressing Brotli data. Any service that unpacks Brotli content it did not create is affected by this issue. Additionally, there are three other high-severity vulnerabilities: CVE-2026-105482, CVE-2026-105483, and CVE-2026-106069. These vulnerabilities compromise Node.js’s ability to verify hostnames and certificates, which is especially important for services that connect to hosts on behalf of users. Three additional points apply to every team: No workarounds are available. Node.js has not published any for these ten CVEs. Upgrading the runtime is the solution. No CVSS scores are available. Currently, the CVE records are reserved and do not have CVSS scores. No updates are available for unsupported lines. Only versions 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x have received fixes. All other versions, including 25.x and 20.x, remain vulnerable and must be upgraded to a supported release. Why Updating Application Dependencies Is Not Enough Updating application dependencies alone will not resolve these issues. The vulnerable code is included in the Node.js runtime, which encompasses runtimes embedded in container images and single-executable applications (SEAs). Node.js also often runs from nonstandard locations: Version managers such as nvm Application folders Bundled runtimes SEAs Container images, running containers, and serverless functions such as AWS Lambda Node.js runtimes What the Vulnerabilities Affect The vulnerabilities span zlib, DNS, TLS, HTTP, crypto, and the Permission Model. Three of the four high-severity issues weaken hostname or certificate validation, which matters for any service that makes outbound TLS or DNS calls on behalf of users. Executive Summary

On October 21, 2026, Node.js released fixes for 10 vulnerabilities across its three supported release lines: 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x. Four are rated High. The most severe, CVE-2026-111497, is an out-of-bounds write in the bundled Brotli decoder that Node.js says permits remote code execution. These flaws live in the Node.js runtime itself, not in application packages, so dependency checks will not surface them. Qualys customers can find affected runtimes across hosts, containers, and cloud workloads, including copies outside standard install paths, prioritize those exposed to the internet, and confirm each fix after patching.

Why This Release Needs Attention Now

The four high-severity vulnerabilities impact two areas that nearly every Node.js service interacts with: compressed data and outbound connections.

CVE-2026-111497 is a vulnerability found in the code responsible for decompressing Brotli data. Any service that unpacks Brotli content it did not create is affected by this issue. Additionally, there are three other high-severity vulnerabilities: CVE-2026-105482, CVE-2026-105483, and CVE-2026-106069. These vulnerabilities compromise Node.js’s ability to verify hostnames and certificates, which is especially important for services that connect to hosts on behalf of users.

Three additional points apply to every team:

  • No workarounds are available. Node.js has not published any for these ten CVEs. Upgrading the runtime is the solution.
  • No CVSS scores are available. Currently, the CVE records are reserved and do not have CVSS scores.

Why Updating Application Dependencies Is Not Enough

Updating application dependencies alone will not resolve these issues. The vulnerable code is included in the Node.js runtime, which encompasses runtimes embedded in container images and single-executable applications (SEAs).

Node.js also often runs from nonstandard locations:

  • Version managers such as nvm
  • Application folders
  • Bundled runtimes
  • SEAs
  • Container images, running containers, and serverless functions such as AWS Lambda Node.js runtimes

The vulnerabilities span zlib, DNS, TLS, HTTP, crypto, and the Permission Model. Three of the four high-severity issues weaken hostname or certificate validation, which matters for any service that makes outbound TLS or DNS calls on behalf of users.

items.summary: The Purview portal ( Audit → Search ) lets you search the Unified Audit Log and export the results to CSV. The full event sits in one column, AuditData, as a JSON blob. To get clean JSON, one event per line, use Exchange Online PowerShell and Search-UnifiedAuditLog. The script is below. Standard audit retention is 180 days; Audit (Premium) keeps a year by default. The Unified Audit Log covers Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams and admin activity in one place. In a business email compromise, it’s where the inbox rules, forwarding and mass downloads show up. Prime Core has 79 detection rules for Microsoft 365 audit data, mapped to 33 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Among them: forwarding rules that siphon mail (T1114.003), extra mailbox permissions (T1098.002) and data pulled from SharePoint (T1213.002). Get Started for Free Before you start Is auditing on? It is by default for most tenants, but check: Connect-ExchangeOnline Get-AdminAuditLogConfig | Format-List UnifiedAuditLogIngestionEnabled True is what you want. If it’s False, nothing was recorded, and turning it on won’t backfill. Roles. You need the Audit Logs or View-Only Audit Logs role. You also need the ExchangeOnlineManagement module (Install-Module ExchangeOnlineManagement). Latency. Events don’t appear instantly. Most show up within an hour or two, some take longer. If you’re chasing something from this morning, it may not be searchable yet. Export with PowerShell Search-UnifiedAuditLog returns at most 5,000 records per call. With a session ID and ReturnLargeSet, you can page through up to 50,000 per search. This loop does that and writes each record’s AuditData, already JSON, as one line: $session = [guid]::NewGuid().ToString() $out = "ual_2026-10-19.jsonl" do { $batch = Search-UnifiedAuditLog -StartDate "2026-10-19 00:00" -EndDate "2026-10-20 00:00" ` -SessionId $session -SessionCommand ReturnLargeSet -ResultSize 5000 $batch | ForEach-Object { $_.AuditData } | Add-Content $out } while ($batch.Count -eq 5000) The log stores times in UTC. Keep that in mind when you set the window. What to look for Operation Why it matters New-InboxRule, Set-InboxRule, UpdateInboxRules Rules that forward, move or delete mail; check the parameters in AuditData Set-Mailbox with ForwardingSmtpAddress Mailbox-level forwarding to an outside address Add-MailboxPermission, Add-RecipientPermission Someone getting access to another mailbox MailItemsAccessed Which messages were actually read; key to scoping a breach FileDownloaded, FileSyncDownloadedFull bursts Bulk download from SharePoint or OneDrive Consent to an application A rogue app granted access to mail or files The classic BEC sequence: a sign-in from a new location, then within minutes an inbox rule that moves replies from the finance team into an obscure folder. Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the .jsonl file. Sanitize. Review. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix Search-UnifiedAuditLog isn’t recognized Not connected to Exchange Online PowerShell Connect-ExchangeOnline first No results Auditing off, events too new, or outside retention Check ingestion; wait; check your audit tier Exactly 5,000 results Per-call limit hit without a session Use the session loop above Stuck at 50,000 Session limit Split the window into smaller pieces Access denied Missing audit role Ask for View-Only Audit Logs FAQ Isn’t this the same as Entra sign-in logs? They overlap: the UAL has UserLoggedIn events. But for authentication details (MFA, Conditional Access, risk), Entra sign-in logs are far richer. Export both. What about the Management Activity API? That’s the route for continuous collection into a SIEM. For a one-off investigation, PowerShell is simpler.

items.summary: GPU teams usually face a bad trade-off. Give every team its own Kubernetes cluster and you pay for a control plane per team. Put everyone in one shared cluster and you get weak isolation. Either way, Kubernetes hands out GPUs as whole cards, so a pod that needs 4 GB of an 80 GB GPU still blocks the entire card. This post shows a way out by combining two open-source projects: Kamaji runs each tenant’s Kubernetes control plane as pods inside one management cluster. HAMi lets pods request a slice of a GPU (memory in MB, compute in %) and packs several pods onto one card. I built the whole thing on a single machine with no physical GPU, using HAMi’s mock device plugin to simulate the cards. The result: two fully isolated tenant clusters, each scheduling fractional-GPU workloads through HAMi, with all eight tests passing. Everything below is reproducible: the exact versions, the commands that worked, the errors I hit and how I fixed them. Architecture One kind cluster hosts Kamaji and both tenant control planes; each tenant’s worker is a separate container that joins over the kind network and runs HAMi. Tenants never share a node or an API server. The only shared pieces are the management cluster and the kamaji-etcd datastore, where each tenant’s data is kept separate. Why Kamaji + HAMi Kamaji solves the cluster problem and HAMi solves the GPU problem; they work at different layers, so they don’t overlap. The interesting part is where they meet. A tenant’s API server lives in the management cluster, but HAMi’s webhook lives on the tenant’s worker nodes. Every GPU pod creation therefore depends on the API server reaching back into the tenant through Kamaji’s Konnectivity tunnel. Proving that path works was the main goal of this lab. Lab setup Everything runs as Docker containers on one Linux host; 4 CPU cores, 8 GB of free RAM and 20 GB of disk are enough. How do you test GPU sharing without a GPU? HAMi’s real device plugin talks to the NVIDIA driver, so it can’t start without hardware. The mock device plugin skips hardware discovery. You describe fake cards in a node annotation, and it registers gpumem and gpucores capacity from that. HAMi’s webhook, scheduler and quota logic then run exactly as they would on real nodes. Joining kindest/node containers works, but Kamaji’s supported route for workers is kubeadm on real machines or Cluster API. Conclusion Kamaji and HAMi fit together without any glue code. The one real integration risk, the hosted API server calling HAMi’s webhook back through Konnectivity, worked on the first try. kubectl annotate node tenant-a-worker hami.io/mutex.lock-

The next pod bound within seconds. This is a mock-only artifact, not a Kamaji or HAMi bug.

What this lab does not prove

The lab proves the wiring and the scheduling decisions, not runtime GPU isolation.

  • No real memory or compute limits. HAMi-core enforces GPU limits inside the container through the NVIDIA driver. A mock card has nothing to enforce.
  • No performance data. No CUDA workloads ran, so throughput and noisy-neighbour effects are untested.
  • Hand-made device data. On real nodes, HAMi’s device plugin writes the node annotation and completes each allocation; here I did both by hand.
  • Unofficial worker path. Joining kindest/node containers works, but Kamaji’s supported route for workers is kubeadm on real machines or Cluster API.
Conclusion

Kamaji and HAMi fit together without any glue code. Kamaji gives each team its own Kubernetes API without a control plane machine per team, and HAMi turns each GPU into a pool of slices inside those clusters. The one real integration risk, the hosted API server calling HAMi’s webhook back through Konnectivity, worked on the first try. If you have no GPU, the mock device plugin is enough to build and test the whole platform before you buy one.

items.title: Hackers Use New BlackX Bootkit to Bypass Windows Secure Boot on Fully Patched Systems
items.summary: A new UEFI bootkit called BlackX has been used in cyberespionage attacks against diplomatic organizations in Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan. The malware targets Secure Boot, a feature designed to help stop untrusted software from running before Windows starts. Researchers say the infected computers had received Windows updates, but a key Secure Boot protection had not been fully applied. Securelist analysts reported the findings on October 22, 2026. They say BlackX uses Baton Drop, a vulnerability tracked as CVE-2022-21894, and shares parts of its design with the BlackLotus bootkit. The findings show why an installed update does not always mean that the protection it is meant to provide has been fully activated. Securelist’s BlackX report describes the malware and the campaign in detail. BlackX is installed after attackers have already gained access to a victim’s network and administrator-level rights. Its installer, inst.exe , works with an encrypted file named PVMDIJGKAX2 , which contains components needed to install the malware. Securelist says this design can make it harder for incident responders to recover all the bootkit’s parts from the installer alone. The bootkit uses Baton Drop to load attacker-controlled EFI files and interfere with Secure Boot. EFI files run during the computer’s startup process, before Windows loads. By gaining a place in that early sequence, a bootkit can give malicious code a chance to run before many operating-system security tools are active. Hackers Use New BlackX Bootkit Readers can learn more about related boot-time risks in this Cybersecurity News report on managing UEFI Secure Boot settings . Securelist says the campaign’s kernel driver attempts to weaken security tools by disrupting process, thread, and registry callbacks, and by interfering with Event Tracing for Windows (ETW), which software can use to collect system activity. It also tries to hide its files: when certain file requests are made, the driver reportedly returns a handle to the legitimate calc.exe process instead of to the requested malicious file. BlackLotus advertisement (Source – Securelist) The bootkit also delivers user-mode malware for espionage. One payload is a remote-access Trojan that can load additional .NET code and use Google Drive, OneDrive, or Yandex.Disk for command-and-control communication. Another, named OxiDLLRunner by the researchers, decrypts a file called v8_context_snapshot.bin and runs a Rust payload that contacts a reported command-and-control domain. The report links the activity to APT41 with medium confidence, based on overlaps with previously reported activity and shared technical details. That assessment is not definitive attribution. Why patched systems were still at risk The issue was not simply that the targeted computers lacked Windows updates. Securelist says the protection against Baton Drop depends on revoking trust in the “Windows Production PCA 2011” certificate used to sign vulnerable UEFI components. Installing an update and applying that revocation are separate steps in the process described by the researchers. Microsoft’s guidance for CVE-2023-24932 also describes multiple steps for deploying Secure Boot protections, including updating certificates, boot managers, and the UEFI revocation list. Its instructions warn that blocking older boot components can affect recovery media and other boot options, so administrators should test changes and prepare recovery options before applying them broadly. See Microsoft’s Secure Boot revocation guidance . The distinction matters because Windows may report that updates are installed even when the firmware’s forbidden-signature list has not yet been updated as intended. Securelist reported that the certificate’s expiration on October 19, 2026, did not by itself stop vulnerable binaries from loading; the certificate must be blocked by the relevant revocation mechanism. Administrators should therefore verify their devices’ Secure Boot configuration and revocation status, following Microsoft’s current instructions and accounting for their organization’s boot and recovery needs. BlackX is not the first bootkit story to raise questions about trust in old boot components. Cybersecurity News has previously covered BlackLotus and how a downgrade technique could leave a Windows device exposed despite an up-to-date status. That background helps explain why Secure Boot protection depends on more than the visible update state of Windows. The main lesson for defenders is to confirm that Secure Boot protections are active in firmware, not only that Windows updates have been installed. Organizations should review Microsoft’s deployment guidance, verify that the necessary revocations have taken effect, and check boot and recovery media for compatibility. Since BlackX was installed after attackers obtained administrator access, teams should also investigate suspicious administrative activity and boot-related changes, and review endpoint alerts for signs that security monitoring has been tampered with. items.title: Compromised TLS Certificates
items.summary: The Indian CA eMudhra Limited has eight TLS certificates with laughably weak private keys : The compromised eMudhra keys were defective at a level that’s challenging the imagination of many of the engineers studying the incident. A normal size for a NIST P-384 elliptic curve cryptography private key contains roughly 384 bits of entropy, a size allowing almost 2 384 , or a number with 116 digits, different possibilities. The private key sizes of the compromised keys ranged from 3 to 8 bits. Astonishingly, the private keys were 4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230, 237. “That is extremely in the ‘this should not be possible’ category,” Valdorda said. “Maybe some horribly dangerous key generation interface has a ‘size’ parameter and they set it to 1 by mistake???” Ben Cartwright-Cox, director of BGP.tools, said: “My guess is that it’s example code that accidentally leaked to production, but hard to know. But it’s bonkers that no one noticed.” At this early stage, the most immediate threat appears to be for those using VPNs, especially in countries with governments likely to maliciously intercept traffic. There are likely many other cases for concern. End users largely have no recourse other than to hold off using many non-browser forms of TLS communication until they receive assurances updates are in place. The whole certificate regime has long been a mess: The incident is the latest to expose a fatal flaw in the TLS regimen. It’s only as strong as its weakest link, which in this case was eMudhra. Fortunately, transparency logs account for much of that failure, but this measure requires parties to actively monitor massive feeds and works only after unauthorized certificates have been issued. eMudhra representatives weren’t immediately available to answer questions. One caveat: exploiting compromised certificates requires an active adversary-in-the-middle attack, meaning the attacker must act as a proxy between two TLS parties and receive encrypted traffic, decrypt it, reencrypt it, and send it to the other party. Such capabilities, in some cases, are usually limited to only the most well-resourced attackers. People with control of a local network­at a coffee shop, university, or other organization­face much less of a challenge. Cleanup of this is going to be another mess—and it’s right on top of the PHP vulnerabilities. Some more information .

items.title: CVE-2026-111497: Node.js Brotli Decoder Flaw Enables Remote Code Execution
items.summary: Node.js has released security updates addressing CVE-2026-111497, a high-severity vulnerability in its bundled Brotli decompression code that can potentially enable remote code execution. The flaw is an out-of-bounds write triggered when a vulnerable decoder processes specially crafted Brotli-compressed data. The issue affects all currently supported Node.js branches—22.x, 24.x, and 26.x. Node.js addressed the vulnerability in versions 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1 as part of the October 21, 2026 security release, which fixed ten vulnerabilities in total. The risk is particularly relevant because Brotli compression is commonly used for HTTP traffic. Node.js applications can invoke the vulnerable decoder directly through node:zlib or automatically when fetch() receives a response using Content-Encoding: br. An application may therefore be exposed whenever attacker-controlled Brotli content reaches the decoder through an inbound request, remote response, proxy workflow, or other data-processing path. For CVE-2026-111497 detection, security teams should prioritize Node.js applications that process untrusted compressed content and monitor them for crashes, abnormal memory behavior, unusual child processes, and suspicious activity immediately following Brotli decompression. Click Explore Detections to access relevant detection content and hunting logic. To Detect CVE-2026-111497, defenders should correlate Node.js application telemetry with endpoint, proxy, web, and network activity to identify suspicious behavior surrounding compressed HTTP traffic. Security teams can also leverage Prime Architect to transform fresh vulnerability intelligence into Sigma rules and hunting queries, validate detection logic, and translate relevant detection content across supported security platforms. Contact Sales CVE-2026-111497 analysis The vulnerability resides in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js. Brotli is a compression algorithm widely used to reduce web content size, and Node.js includes its own copy of the library. A malformed compressed stream can trigger an out-of-bounds write, causing the decoder to write outside the memory buffer allocated for decompressed data. The upstream fix changes the decoder so that invalid input is rejected earlier instead of allowing execution to continue into the unsafe memory-write condition. CVE-2026-111497 affects Node.js 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x before the October 21 security releases. The patched versions are: Node.js 22.23.4 Node.js 24.22.1 Node.js 26.12.1 Node.js 20.x and earlier releases have reached end of life and do not receive the security update, so organizations using those versions should migrate to a supported branch. The underlying problem is not limited to Node.js. The vulnerable code comes from the Brotli project itself, and the corresponding fixes were released in Brotli 1.0.10, 1.1.1, and 1.2.1. Other applications that embed vulnerable Brotli versions may therefore need separate updates even if they do not use Node.js. The attack surface depends on how compressed data reaches the application. Direct use of Brotli decompression APIs is one obvious route. However, Node.js can also automatically process Brotli-compressed HTTP responses when applications use fetch(). This makes applications that retrieve attacker-controlled content especially relevant. Examples include URL preview services, crawlers, webhook processors, proxy platforms, content scanners, conversion services, and applications that allow users to submit remote URLs. Inbound traffic can create another path where a web application or middleware accepts Brotli-compressed request bodies. Security teams should therefore examine actual application data flows rather than limiting exposure assessment to explicit Brotli calls in source code. The details for CVE-2026-111497 show why the issue can have consequences beyond a simple service crash. Memory corruption can potentially affect nearby process state and, depending on platform protections and runtime conditions, lead to memory disclosure or arbitrary code execution. Node.js explicitly describes the vulnerability as capable of remote code execution, but its practical exploitability deserves nuance. The flaw is rated High by the Node.js Project rather than Critical. A public CVE-2026-111497 PoC released after disclosure achieved code execution against a deliberately weakened test build. Against a standard Node.js build, the researcher reported a crash and limited process-memory disclosure but did not achieve reliable code execution. This means the memory-corruption primitive is demonstrated, while successful RCE against normal production builds depends on additional exploit conditions. Patched Node.js versions reject the malformed content used in the demonstration. As of October 22, no exploitation in the wild had been reported. Accordingly, campaign-specific CVE-2026-111497 IOCs such as malicious IP addresses, domains, payload hashes, or confirmed exploit request signatures have not been published in the cited research. Security teams should instead focus on behavioral indicators such as: Unexpected crashes of Node.js services handling compressed traffic Segmentation faults or native decoder failures Abnormal memory-protection or exploit-prevention alerts Node.js spawning shells or command interpreters Unusual outbound connections immediately after Brotli processing Suspicious compressed requests from unfamiliar sources Server-side fetch() activity reaching untrusted infrastructure Unexpected file or process changes originating from a Node.js service account The October 21 Node.js release also fixed additional high-severity issues involving TLS hostname validation and DNS processing. CybersecurityNews notes that organizations should treat the release as a broader runtime security update rather than focusing exclusively on the Brotli flaw. The same release also refreshed certificate trust information following the eMudhra certificate authority compromise, further increasing the value of upgrading rather than attempting to backport only one fix. CVE-2026-111497 Mitigation The primary CVE-2026-111497 mitigation is to upgrade all supported Node.js installations to a patched version: 22.x → 22.23.4 or later 24.x → 24.22.1 or later 26.x → 26.12.1 or later The Node.js Project provides no equivalent temporary runtime workaround for the Brotli vulnerability, making upgrading the reliable remediation path. After updating the runtime, administrators should restart all affected Node.js services. Long-running processes continue using the old runtime until restarted. Containerized workloads require additional attention. CybersecurityNews specifically recommends rebuilding container images so deployed applications contain the patched Node.js runtime. Updating Node.js on the underlying host does not replace a vulnerable runtime already embedded inside a container image. Organizations using Brotli independently should also update vulnerable library versions. Software inventories and SBOMs can help identify embedded copies in native applications, appliances, development tools, and third-party packages. Where immediate upgrading is not possible, organizations can temporarily reduce attack surface by: Rejecting Brotli-compressed request bodies where compression is unnecessary Restricting server-side HTTP requests to trusted destinations Preventing users from supplying arbitrary remote URLs Limiting outbound connectivity from vulnerable workloads Disabling optional Brotli processing where operationally feasible Monitoring application crashes and memory-related errors closely Inspecting unusual child processes launched by Node.js Vercel introduced firewall protections to block malicious Brotli data arriving through inbound requests. However, The Hacker News notes that those rules do not protect applications that independently fetch malicious Brotli responses from external servers, illustrating why WAF filtering cannot replace the runtime upgrade. Administrators should also confirm the runtime actually used by production workloads after patching. Package-manager output alone is insufficient when older Node.js binaries remain inside containers, serverless bundles, packaged applications, or manually installed runtime directories. If exploitation is suspected, responders should isolate the affected workload and preserve application, endpoint, proxy, and network telemetry. Crash dumps may be especially valuable because the vulnerability directly affects process memory. Security teams should investigate: Unexpected Node.js child processes Newly created files or persistence mechanisms Unusual outbound connections Changes to application or deployment configuration Credentials and secrets available in environment variables API keys, tokens, and cloud credentials accessible to the Node.js process Backend data stores reachable using the application’s service identity Because limited process-memory disclosure has been demonstrated, secrets resident in the vulnerable application’s memory should be considered potentially exposed when suspicious exploitation activity is identified, even if arbitrary code execution cannot be conclusively proven. Organizations should also review the privileges assigned to affected services. Successful exploitation of a minimally privileged container has different consequences from exploitation of a Node.js process holding cloud credentials, database administrative access, CI/CD tokens, or deployment permissions. SOC Prime customers can leverage behavior-based detection content to identify vulnerability exploitation and related attacker activity while vulnerable systems are discovered and remediated. Disclaimer: Detection content may not be available for every CVE. Check the SOC Prime Platform for current coverage. If relevant detections are not yet available, check again as new threat intelligence and detection content are continuously added. FAQ What is CVE-2026-111497 and how does it work? CVE-2026-111497 is an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the Brotli decoder included with Node.js. A maliciously constructed Brotli stream can cause the decoder to write beyond its intended memory buffer. Depending on the environment and exploitation conditions, this can lead to a process crash, disclosure of process memory, or potentially execution of attacker-controlled code. The vulnerable decoder may be reached through direct decompression APIs or automatically when Node.js processes Brotli-compressed HTTP responses. When was CVE-2026-111497 first discovered? The Node.js Project publicly disclosed and patched the vulnerability on October 21, 2026. OpenAI Codex Security researchers Khai Tran and Sylvie Mayer are credited with reporting the issue to Node.js. The Hacker News reports that the corresponding Brotli source-code change was first made upstream in February 2026 but was distributed as a security fix in October. What is the impact of CVE-2026-111497 on systems? Successful exploitation can corrupt memory within a vulnerable Node.js process. Possible consequences include denial of service through application crashes, exposure of process memory, and potentially remote code execution. The actual impact depends on whether attacker-controlled Brotli content reaches the decoder and whether the memory-corruption primitive can bypass protections in the target runtime and operating system. If code execution is achieved, the attacker would generally inherit the permissions and access available to the compromised Node.js process, potentially exposing application data, credentials, cloud resources, or connected backend systems. Can CVE-2026-111497 still affect me in 2026? Yes. Node.js 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x installations remain vulnerable if they have not been updated to the October 21 patched releases. Organizations running Node.js 20.x or older should migrate to a supported release because end-of-life branches do not receive this fix. Applications that embed vulnerable Brotli libraries independently may also remain exposed even if Node.js itself has been updated. How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-111497? Upgrade Node.js to 22.23.4, 24.22.1, 26.12.1, or a newer supported release and restart affected workloads. Rebuild container images, update independently bundled Brotli libraries, and verify that production services are actually running the patched binaries. Until patching is complete, reduce exposure to untrusted Brotli input and restrict server-side requests to approved destinations. Monitor vulnerable services for crashes, unusual child processes, unexpected network activity, and other signs of memory exploitation. If suspicious activity is discovered, isolate the workload, preserve forensic evidence, and rotate sensitive credentials available to the affected Node.js process.

The October 21 Node.js release also fixed additional high-severity issues involving TLS hostname validation and DNS processing. CybersecurityNews notes that organizations should treat the release as a broader runtime security update rather than focusing exclusively on the Brotli flaw.

The same release also refreshed certificate trust information following the eMudhra certificate authority compromise, further increasing the value of upgrading rather than attempting to backport only one fix.

CVE-2026-111497 Mitigation

The primary CVE-2026-111497 mitigation is to upgrade all supported Node.js installations to a patched version:

  • 22.x → 22.23.4 or later
  • 24.x → 24.22.1 or later
  • 26.x → 26.12.1 or later

The Node.js Project provides no equivalent temporary runtime workaround for the Brotli vulnerability, making upgrading the reliable remediation path.

After updating the runtime, administrators should restart all affected Node.js services. Long-running processes continue using the old runtime until restarted.

Containerized workloads require additional attention. CybersecurityNews specifically recommends rebuilding container images so deployed applications contain the patched Node.js runtime. Updating Node.js on the underlying host does not replace a vulnerable runtime already embedded inside a container image.

Organizations using Brotli independently should also update vulnerable library versions. Software inventories and SBOMs can help identify embedded copies in native applications, appliances, development tools, and third-party packages.

Where immediate upgrading is not possible, organizations can temporarily reduce attack surface by:

  • Rejecting Brotli-compressed request bodies where compression is unnecessary
  • Restricting server-side HTTP requests to trusted destinations
  • Preventing users from supplying arbitrary remote URLs
  • Limiting outbound connectivity from vulnerable workloads
  • Disabling optional Brotli processing where operationally feasible
  • Monitoring application crashes and memory-related errors closely
  • Inspecting unusual child processes launched by Node.js

Vercel introduced firewall protections to block malicious Brotli data arriving through inbound requests. However, The Hacker News notes that those rules do not protect applications that independently fetch malicious Brotli responses from external servers, illustrating why WAF filtering cannot replace the runtime upgrade.

Administrators should also confirm the runtime actually used by production workloads after patching. Package-manager output alone is insufficient when older Node.js binaries remain inside containers, serverless bundles, packaged applications, or manually installed runtime directories.

If exploitation is suspected, responders should isolate the affected workload and preserve application, endpoint, proxy, and network telemetry. Crash dumps may be especially valuable because the vulnerability directly affects process memory.

Security teams should investigate:

  • Unexpected Node.js child processes
  • Newly created files or persistence mechanisms
  • Unusual outbound connections
  • Changes to application or deployment configuration
  • Credentials and secrets available in environment variables
  • API keys, tokens, and cloud credentials accessible to the Node.js process
  • Backend data stores reachable using the application’s service identity

Because limited process-memory disclosure has been demonstrated, secrets resident in the vulnerable application’s memory should be considered potentially exposed when suspicious exploitation activity is identified, even if arbitrary code execution cannot be conclusively proven.

Organizations should also review the privileges assigned to affected services. Successful exploitation of a minimally privileged container has different consequences from exploitation of a Node.js process holding cloud credentials, database administrative access, CI/CD tokens, or deployment permissions.

FAQ

What is CVE-2026-111497 and how does it work?

CVE-2026-111497 is an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the Brotli decoder included with Node.js. A maliciously constructed Brotli stream can cause the decoder to write beyond its intended memory buffer. Depending on the environment and exploitation conditions, this can lead to a process crash, disclosure of process memory, or potentially execution of attacker-controlled code. The vulnerable decoder may be reached through direct decompression APIs or automatically when Node.js processes Brotli-compressed HTTP responses.

When was CVE-2026-111497 first discovered?

The Node.js Project publicly disclosed and patched the vulnerability on October 21, 2026. OpenAI Codex Security researchers Khai Tran and Sylvie Mayer are credited with reporting the issue to Node.js. The Hacker News reports that the corresponding Brotli source-code change was first made upstream in February 2026 but was distributed as a security fix in October.

What is the impact of CVE-2026-111497 on systems?

Successful exploitation can corrupt memory within a vulnerable Node.js process. Possible consequences include denial of service through application crashes, exposure of process memory, and potentially remote code execution. The actual impact depends on whether attacker-controlled Brotli content reaches the decoder and whether the memory-corruption primitive can bypass protections in the target runtime and operating system. If code execution is achieved, the attacker would generally inherit the permissions and access available to the compromised Node.js process, potentially exposing application data, credentials, cloud resources, or connected backend systems.

Can CVE-2026-111497 still affect me in 2026?

Yes. Node.js 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x installations remain vulnerable if they have not been updated to the October 21 patched releases. Organizations running Node.js 20.x or older should migrate to a supported release because end-of-life branches do not receive this fix. Applications that embed vulnerable Brotli libraries independently may also remain exposed even if Node.js itself has been updated.

How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-111497?

Upgrade Node.js to 22.23.4, 24.22.1, 26.12.1, or a newer supported release and restart affected workloads. Rebuild container images, update independently bundled Brotli libraries, and verify that production services are actually running the patched binaries. Until patching is complete, reduce exposure to untrusted Brotli input and restrict server-side requests to approved destinations. Monitor vulnerable services for crashes, unusual child processes, unexpected network activity, and other signs of memory exploitation. If suspicious activity is discovered, isolate the workload, preserve forensic evidence, and rotate sensitive credentials available to the affected Node.js process.

items.title: Crime Stoppers chapter freezes tips after breach breaks anonymity promise
items.summary: A breach exposed personal information in supposedly anonymous crime reports. Now one Crime Stoppers chapter has stopped accepting tips because it cannot guarantee anonymity. Toronto Crime Stoppers, which works with the community, police, and media to help solve crimes, has paused phone, website, and app submissions while it seeks a safer system. The breach occurred in March and involved P3 Global Intel, the Texas-based tip-management platform owned by Navigate360. Its software is used by Crime Stoppers programs and other organizations in the US and elsewhere. An October CBC investigation revealed the Canadian impact: More than 1.5 million tips spanning 25 years were exposed, with over 850,000 containing personal information. That included addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, and some banking details associated with rewards. The exposed details belonged to tipsters, people named in allegations, and others, including police and Crime Stoppers staff. Following CBC’s reporting, Toronto Crime Stoppers acknowledged that its promise of anonymity had been broken for some users. The organization stopped accepting tips, saying it could no longer guarantee users’ anonymity. In an October 21 statement , the organization says identifying details are normally removed before tips reach investigators, but some original submissions containing potentially identifying information were stolen from P3. For affected tipsters, exposure could create a risk of retaliation, intimidation, or extortion. Scammers could also use details of a genuine tip to make an approach more convincing. Unfortunately, the pause removes a reporting option for people afraid to approach police. Toronto police still accept reports directly, but warn that those channels are not anonymous. How to stay safe Toronto Crime Stoppers warned people worried about exposure to watch for impersonators. It says it will never contact them first to request a tip number, password, or other information. The statement did not describe an individual notification process or offer a way to check whether a particular tip was affected. For anyone wanting to submit a new tip, the organization’s message was clear: “Until we have a safer way to protect you, please do not send us tips by phone, online, or through the app.” Anyone in immediate danger should call 911. During the pause, non-emergency reports in Toronto should go directly to Toronto police, with the understanding that those channels are not anonymous. If you use a different Crime Stoppers program, check its official website for updates and advice about its reporting system. For more general advice if your information may have been exposed, read our blog “ Involved in a data breach? Here’s what you need to know .” What do cybercriminals know about you? items.title: SBI Notifies Customers Impacted by the Recent Cyber Incident
items.summary: State Bank of India (SBI) has individually notified customers whose information was identified in a recent cyber incident, sending alerts through email and WhatsApp. In its latest advisory on October 23 , the bank said customer account balances and funds remain safe while investigators examine the suspected exposure of personal information found on the dark web. The update shifts the bank’s response from an initial public disclosure to direct communication with customers. According to The Economic Times, SBI said it had informed all customers whose data was identified as involved. The bank also warned users to stay alert for suspicious calls, messages, and emails, and never share passwords, PINs, or one-time passwords. SBI’s preliminary review examined approximately 375,000 records available on the dark web and identified 3,897 customer records containing personally identifiable information. These figures represent different measures. The larger number describes the records reviewed, not a confirmed count of affected SBI customers or compromised bank accounts. SBI Notifies Customers Impacted By Cyber Incident The information reportedly included names, registered mobile numbers, dates of birth, email addresses and home addresses. Other fields included gender, branch details, Customer Information File identifiers, and information linked to loan inquiries and lead records. These details can identify customers and provide context about their banking relationships. pic.twitter.com/lrIZtM5nnQ — State Bank of India (@TheOfficialSBI) October 23, 2026 As covered in Cybersecurity News’ earlier report on the SBI data loss incident , the disclosure did not establish how the information was obtained. It also did not confirm that attackers had entered SBI’s core banking systems. No publicly identified entry point, exploited software flaw, or malware family explained the incident. SBI received alerts on October 16 from its threat intelligence service provider, the Defense Cyber Agency, and the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team, known as CERT-In. The bank activated its incident response and containment procedures and appointed an independent cybersecurity agency impaneled with CERT-In to investigate. Investigators are examining the authenticity, source and extent of the exposed information. SBI has said the incident caused no material impact on its core operations, financial performance or business continuity. Banking services continued without disruption, according to the bank’s disclosure. An earlier unverified claim about an SBI data breach alleged that customer records and banking documents had been posted online. Those allegations should remain separate from SBI’s confirmed findings while the investigation continues. Personal data exposure does not automatically mean an account has been taken over. Available reporting does not establish that passwords, PINs, OTPs, or transaction credentials were compromised. However, exposed contact and loan details could help criminals create convincing messages that appear to come from the bank. Customers should verify unexpected notifications through official banking channels rather than trust a message because it contains accurate personal details. They should avoid unfamiliar links and check statements for unauthorized transactions. SBI’s official cybersecurity guidance lists report.phishing@sbi.co.in for reporting cyber incidents and directs users to India’s cybercrime helpline, 1930. The bank’s latest warning stresses that customers must never disclose authentication codes or banking passwords to anyone. Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. items.title: Hackers Exploit Critical Citrix NetScaler RCE Flaw to Deploy Web Shells and Malware
items.summary: A critical vulnerability in Citrix NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway is being exploited to run commands on exposed appliances, install web shells and deliver malware. Tracked as CVE-2026-88771, the flaw allows an unauthenticated attacker to execute commands remotely. Citrix disclosed it on September 27, 2026, and confirmed exploitation of appliances that had not been protected by an update. The vulnerability is rated 9.8 under CVSS v3.1 and 9.5 under CVSS v4.0, according to the Zscaler ThreatLabz report. The activity is concerning because NetScaler devices often sit at the edge of company networks and handle remote access or application traffic. A web shell can provide a way back into a compromised appliance, while a separate malware implant can give attackers another foothold. The campaign also shows why applying a patch alone may not be enough: organizations need to check whether attackers already changed files, settings or system logs. Researchers from Zscaler ThreatLabz identified a staged exploitation chain that used log poisoning, command execution, attempts to place web shells and delivery of a FreeBSD malware implant. Their technical analysis of CVE-2026-88771 says the attackers first placed encoded content in web access logs, then sent crafted authentication requests designed to trigger a vulnerable diagnostic process. Hackers Exploit Critical Citrix NetScaler RCE Flaw In the observed activity, requests to common NetScaler web paths carried a distinctive “INDEX:” marker and encoded content in the User-Agent field. These requests were intended to get attacker-controlled data written to access logs; the initial request did not itself run the full payload. Attackers then sent authentication requests containing text made to resemble a Packet Processing Engine failure message. The vulnerable process, a Perl diagnostic script, later handled matching log entries. According to Zscaler, the script did not safely handle attacker-controlled characters in the forged message. When the script processed a poisoned entry, appended commands could run with its privileges. This delayed method helps explain why a request that appears to be ordinary web or login traffic may be part of a larger attempt to compromise an appliance. Attack chain (Source – Zscaler) The observed payloads attempted to create web-accessible files, enable PHP or Perl handling in the web server, and install files named Nx_7508.php and Nx_7508.pl . Researchers also saw attempts to download and run a 64-bit FreeBSD binary named kw2-freebsd-x64-s11 . Zscaler reported that the download infrastructure had also appeared in activity targeting Magento and Adobe Commerce with CVE-2026-75650, known as StyleSmuggler. That overlap is an investigative lead, not proof that the same threat actor carried out both campaigns. This is not the first time attackers have used NetScaler flaws to leave behind web shells. Cyber Security News previously reported on web shells on hacked Citrix NetScalers and a separate campaign involving Citrix NetScaler zero-days and malware . These earlier reports are useful context, but they concern different incidents and should not be treated as evidence that the same operators are responsible. What organizations should do Citrix’s fixed builds listed in the Zscaler report are NetScaler ADC and Gateway 14.1-73.46 or later, and 13.1-64.29 or later. The report also lists 14.1-73.46 FIPS or later for 14.1-FIPS, and 13.1.37.283 or later for 13.1-FIPS and 13.1-NDcPP. Administrators should verify the correct build for their product and upgrade promptly. Before updating, preserve relevant evidence where possible, including remote syslog data, technical support bundles and available core dumps. Then review authentication and web access logs for suspicious “INDEX:” User-Agent values, forged “pitboss PPE” failure messages, unexpected requests to the paths listed below, and appliance-initiated connections to unfamiliar hosts. Also inspect for unapproved web files, changed web-server settings and suspicious processes. If compromise is suspected, isolate the appliance while preserving evidence and rotate credentials, tokens and certificates it could access. Patching prevents further exploitation of the flaw, but does not by itself remove an existing web shell or implant. items.title: Hacker With Limited Skills Used DeepSeek AI to Breach Indian University and Steal Over 5,200 Records
items.summary: A cybercriminal using the online handle BUGSTER used artificial intelligence tools to support attacks on Indian organizations, including two universities. In one confirmed intrusion, the attacker stole a MongoDB database containing more than 5,200 records, including personal information about students and staff, according to Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42. The researchers did not name the universities. The actor’s setup combined Hermes Agent, an AI assistant framework, with DeepSeek V4 as its reasoning model and Cursor as a coding tool. Unit 42 said the attacker turned off safety controls and relied on AI-written scripts and reports. The case shows how AI can help a person with limited skills take on tasks that once demanded more experience, though it does not mean the model carried out the activity on its own. Analysts from Unit 42 identified and investigated the activity by examining the operator’s environment, tools and records. They found evidence of activity beyond the university intrusions, including credential theft, Wi-Fi password cracking, cryptocurrency research, and plans for phone-service fraud. Hacker With Limited Skills Used DeepSeek AI At one university, the actor used AI-assisted research to map an online education platform and its related services. The report described a WordPress site, a learning platform, a student portal and an administration dashboard. The actor then used the information to try account passwords, and the tool identified one working login. Unit 42 did not say that this activity led to the theft of the 5,200 records; that database came from a separate university intrusion. Example of a WordPress REST API enumeration report from the activity (Source – Unit42) In the second case, the actor accessed a public university’s database with an administrator account protected by a weak password. The stolen MongoDB data included student records from diploma, undergraduate and postgraduate programs, as well as faculty information. The actor’s records also showed details about parts of the university’s cloud and database setup. These incidents show why an exposed service or weak account can have serious effects, even without a newly discovered software flaw. The activity described by Unit 42 relied on basic tools, information gathered about the targets and access to an administrator account. Readers following DeepSeek-powered Hermes Agent attacks can compare this case with another report on AI-assisted activity involving the same tools. AI supported work across several schemes Unit 42 said the actor used AI-generated reports to organize research and produce scripts. Investigators also found a large credential-scanning toolkit designed to look for exposed secrets, such as cloud keys and private keys in files or logs. This kind of information can give criminals access to services if an organization has left it unprotected. The actor also built AI profiles for separate tasks. One profile was used to seek advice about VoIP fraud, while another researched phone carriers. Unit 42 found planning material but no call records or signs that the phone operation had become active. This distinction matters: the report documents preparation and research, not proof that the planned fraud was carried out. Other activity included an automated process for trying to crack Wi-Fi passwords. Unit 42 said it required a device near the target networks to collect authentication data, suggesting the actor had local access to the locations. The actor also collected information about large cryptocurrency holders, but researchers did not find evidence of follow-up activity against them. Using the pandarouter profile to investigate a carrier (Source – Unit42) Related reporting on DeepSeek safety research findings covers concerns about AI models producing harmful guidance. Unit 42’s findings add a different point: an attacker can combine an AI model with ordinary tools and weak account security to pursue several types of crime. Universities and other organizations should review administrator accounts, remove weak or reused passwords, and require multi-factor authentication where possible. They should also limit database access to approved systems and users, check internet-facing portals for unnecessary exposure, and monitor account activity for unusual login attempts or access to large sets of records. Organizations should protect secrets such as API keys and cloud credentials by keeping them out of public files and logs. If a credential may have been exposed, teams should revoke or rotate it, then review access records for signs of misuse. These steps address the security gaps described in the report; they do not depend on identifying a particular AI model. The activity also highlights the value of monitoring what AI agents can access. If AI tools are used for legitimate work, organizations should limit their permissions, keep safety and approval controls enabled, and review their actions. The case is part of a wider set of reported concerns about AI-enabled cybercrime, including DeepSeek-powered credential theft activity . items.title: Oracle Issues Emergency Java Update for Critical 9.1 HTTPS Trust Vulnerability
items.summary: Oracle has released an emergency Java security update to address CVE-2026-91403, a critical vulnerability affecting how Java applications trust digital certificates. Published on October 21, 2026, the alert assigns the flaw a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.1 and covers Oracle Java SE and GraalVM. The update blocks affected intermediate certificate authority certificates linked to eMudhra. According to Oracle’s security advisory, the issue affects the Java Secure Socket Extension, or JSSE, component. Oracle rates exploitation as low complexity, with no authentication or user interaction required. Successful attacks can expose or change sensitive data, although the risk matrix lists no availability impact. The problem involves certificate chains that Java uses to decide whether a remote service is trusted. Red Hat explains that eMudhra issued intermediate certificates with weak private keys. An attacker positioned between a Java client and a server could use those weak keys to create certificates for arbitrary hostnames, making a malicious site appear trusted. This undermines the identity checks behind HTTPS. Encryption alone cannot protect a connection when the client accepts an attacker’s certificate as valid. The fix therefore changes which certificates Java accepts, rather than removing HTTPS support or replacing the entire certificate system. Oracle’s update specifically distrusts the impacted intermediate certificates. Affected Java and GraalVM Versions Oracle lists Java SE 8u511, 8u511-perf, 11.0.33, 17.0.21, 21.0.13, 25.0.5, and 27.0.1 as affected. GraalVM for JDK 17.0.21 and 21.0.13, alongside GraalVM Enterprise Edition 21.3.20, are also included. Earlier releases may be vulnerable, but unsupported versions were not tested. Oracle notes that affected APIs can be reached through services supplying data to JSSE. Its advisory also covers certain sandboxed Java Web Start applications and applets that load untrusted code. The announcement does not report confirmed attacks exploiting this vulnerability. Oracle recommends installing the latest Java update or following its eMudhra mitigation instructions . Teams unable to update immediately can replace the local blocked.certs file with Oracle’s supplied version, preserving existing custom entries. Java 8 requires the replacement file to be named blacklisted.certs . Alternatively, Oracle advises enabling TLS revocation checks using -Dcom.sun.net.ssl.checkRevocation=true and -Dcom.sun.security.enableCRLDP=true . For signed JAR verification on JDK 17 and later, it provides jarsigner -verify -revcheck -strict [SIGNED_JAR] . These are alternatives, not steps that must all be applied together. The emergency alert follows Oracle’s wider patching efforts, including its September security update and August security patches . However, administrators should check this specific advisory rather than assume earlier updates cover the certificate issue. Oracle directs customers to its patch availability document for installation details and recommends moving unsupported deployments to supported releases. items.title: PwC Data Breach Claim – Everest Ransomware Group Claims to Have Stolen 590 GB of Data
items.summary: The Everest ransomware group claims to have stolen 590.69 GB of data from PwC, the global professional services firm. This alleged data theft includes human resources records, training materials, and internal documents. However, the claims are unverified, and PwC has not yet responded. The group’s listing was reported on October 22, 2026. Hackmanac’s public alert described 108,426 files allegedly taken from internal HR and learning systems. Separately, CTIWatch’s victim tracker recorded PwC appearing on Everest’s leak site that day. These reports document the claim, not independent proof of a breach. Alleged PwC Data Breach The supplied leak-site screenshot names a directory, pwc-stg.csod.com , and describes Cornerstone OnDemand platform materials, regional HR exports, e-learning courses, and integration testing documents. It lists 494 directories, alongside 1,333 original archive containers and 53 nested containers. The screenshot alone does not establish how these materials were obtained. Hackmanac reported that the alleged data spans PwC operations in Australia, China, Canada, and the UK. One HR dataset reportedly contains 213,084 records. That figure should not be read as a confirmed count of affected employees because the number of unique people remains unknown. The alert also mentions employee information, employment and training records, internal audit methods, confidential documents, and single sign-on source code and configuration files. It does not establish whether working passwords, tokens, or other usable secrets are present. PwC Data Breach Claim The screenshot threatens publication after a countdown and urges the company to make contact. A reported October 28 release deadline has not been independently confirmed. No ransom amount, initial access method, or evidence of encrypted PwC systems has been established in the reviewed material. Everest has previously used data theft claims to pressure named organizations, including its alleged McDonald’s India breach . However, its history includes both data extortion and file encryption, so this listing should not automatically be treated as proof of ransomware deployment. A separate technical analysis of Everest ransomware found no data theft function inside one examined encryptor. Researchers noted that any theft could instead occur earlier through separate tools. That finding does not explain this alleged incident. If authentic, detailed employee records could help criminals craft convincing phishing messages or impersonate staff. items.title: Critical Cisco Expressway Vulnerability Enables Remote Code Execution Attacks
items.summary: Cisco has released security updates for a critical Cisco Expressway vulnerability that could let remote attackers run operating system commands as root. Tracked as CVE-2026-76466, the flaw carries a CVSS score of 9.8 and affects vulnerable Expressway devices configured in a cluster. Cisco published its advisory on October 21, 2026. The issue affects Cisco Expressway Core (Expressway-C) and Cisco Expressway Edge (Expressway-E). Both virtual deployments and hardware appliances are affected when running vulnerable software with clustering enabled. Successful exploitation could give attackers control over the underlying operating system. According to Cisco’s security advisory , the weakness sits in the database service and involves persistent cookies. Cisco also found that client certificates are not properly checked when clustering enables TLS Verify Mode. This means the enabled setting does not provide the expected certificate validation. An attacker who has the required cookies and network access to an affected device could connect to its database service and invoke specific remote procedure call commands. These calls could allow the attacker to run commands with root privileges , the highest level of access on the system. Cisco Expressway Vulnerability Although Cisco describes the attacker as unauthenticated, possession of the cookies remains an important requirement. The advisory does not explain how an attacker would obtain them. Readers should therefore avoid interpreting the finding as proof that an attacker can immediately compromise every reachable Expressway device. The potential impact resembles other cases covered in Cyber Security News’ reporting on critical Cisco remote code execution flaws , though the affected products and attack methods differ. Cisco lists Expressway X15.5.3 and earlier as affected, with X15.5.20 identified as the first fixed release. Customers using X14 or earlier must migrate to a fixed release. No workarounds address this vulnerability. The fix is also included in Cisco’s broader October 2026 Expressway security hardening release. That release addresses additional weaknesses discovered during an internal security review. Unlike this cluster-specific flaw, the broader hardening advisory covers affected Expressway-C and Expressway-E devices regardless of configuration. Administrators should check installed versions and cluster settings, then plan upgrades using Cisco’s compatibility guidance. Checking the version alone does not establish exposure because this particular vulnerability also requires a clustered deployment. Broader coverage is available through Cyber Security News’ Cisco security updates . Cisco credited Stefan Aleksic of Jane Street with reporting the vulnerability. At publication, its Product Security Incident Response Team said it was unaware of public announcements or malicious use. That statement does not reduce the need to patch affected clusters, given the potential for remote commands to run as root. Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. items.title: Splunk Fixes 24 Security Flaws, Including Four Critical Vulnerabilities in Enterprise and SOAR
items.summary: Splunk has released security updates for 24 vulnerabilities in Splunk Enterprise and Splunk SOAR , including four critical flaws with CVSS scores from 9.3 to 9.9. CVE-2026-76300, scored 8.8, concerns poor control of a resource during its lifetime, while CVE-2026-76301 carries a 7.6 score for a protection failure. Splunk groups internal findings by weakness type so that each CVE may represent more than one related issue. The Splunk SOAR advisory lists eight CVEs fixed in version 8.7.0. The most serious is CVE-2026-76531, rated 9.9, which may leave files or directories open to outside parties. CVE-2026-76407 is another critical issue with a 9.3 score and involves improper access control. items.title: Critical Unpatched Linux Kernel Flaws Accidentally Disclosed on Public List
items.summary: Several unpatched Linux-related security flaws were posted to public mailing lists in October, exposing technical details before fixes were ready. The reports, submitted by Trend Micro’s Zero Day Initiative (ZDI), include two critical flaws rated CVSS 9.0 that could let a remote attacker run code on systems using the Linux kernel’s KSMBD file server. Other reports describe local privilege-escalation and information-disclosure risks. The reports appeared on public lists, and Linux kernel maintainer Greg Kroah-Hartman questioned why some submissions were sent there without patches. But the reports credit Trend Micro’s AI scanner, and reporting on the disclosure points to updated kernel guidance that treats AI-found bugs as already public. ZDI had not publicly explained the routing as of October 23, 2026, so it remains unclear whether this was a simple mistake. Two Critical Flaws Affect KSMBD The most urgent reports concern KSMBD, an optional SMB file server built into the Linux kernel. It is separate from Samba, the commonly used file-sharing software. That means the reports do not automatically affect Linux systems running Samba alone. The immediate question for operators is whether KSMBD is enabled and serving files. ZDI-CAN-33774 describes a race condition in KSMBD that could lead to remote code execution. A race condition occurs when the outcome depends on the timing of tasks running at the same time. In this case, the report says that a mismatch in how the server handles queued network requests may lead to memory being read or written beyond its intended limits. ZDI rated the flaw CVSS 9.0. ZDI-CAN-33549 , also rated CVSS 9.0, affects KSMBD’s SMB Direct path. The reported cause is an integer underflow: a size value can wrap around after a subtraction, leaving the program with an incorrect length. A later memory operation may then exceed its buffer. The issue concerns SMB Direct, which uses RDMA networking, so exposure depends on the server’s configuration and use of that feature. A fix was reportedly present in a development branch intended for Linux 7.5, but that does not mean it was already available in released or distribution kernels. At the time of reporting, neither critical issue had a named fix in the mainline kernel or its integration tree, and no CVE identifier had been assigned. Kernel changes also need to reach stable and distribution releases before many users can install them. Administrators should therefore check their Linux vendor’s security notices rather than assume that a fix in a development branch has reached their systems. Four Other Reports Cover Different Components The remaining reports do not all affect the same part of Linux. ZDI-CAN-33367 involves the skb_zerocopy networking code and may allow a local user to gain higher privileges. Kernel developers had reportedly received a separate report about the same issue the previous week, with a patch expected. ZDI-CAN-34068 concerns an out-of-bounds write in the VMware graphics driver, which could also enable local privilege escalation. ZDI-CAN-34076 involves an uninitialized resource in the NVMe over Fabrics target code and may expose information. ZDI-CAN-32005 , posted a day earlier, is a stack-buffer overflow in ConnMan’s handling of search-domain TCP queries. ConnMan is a network-management service, not a Linux kernel component, so this report should not be described as a kernel flaw. Start by checking whether KSMBD is active and whether the system needs it. If it is not required, disabling it reduces exposure to the two remote-code-execution reports. If it is needed, keep file-sharing services away from untrusted networks, review share access, and monitor the Linux distribution’s security updates for fixes. These steps reduce risk but do not replace installing a vendor-approved patch once it becomes available. The reports also show why public disclosure before a fix can create pressure for maintainers and system operators. Public details can help defenders understand what to check, but they can also give attackers useful information before updates reach users. For context on earlier KSMBD risks, see Cyber Security News’ coverage of a Linux KSMBD remote-code-execution flaw and its report on an AI-assisted discovery in the Linux SMB server . For ongoing protection, administrators should follow their distribution’s advisories and apply fixes as soon as they are released. Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears.
